chunks: From him, from Aban, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

Iblis, on the Day of Badr, used to make the Muslims appear few in the eyes of the disbelievers, and make the disbelievers appear many in the eyes of the Muslims. So Jibreel (peace be upon him) struck him with the sword, and he fled from him while saying, 'O Jibreel, I am granted respite, I am granted respite,' until he fell into the sea.
Zurara said: 'So I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'Why was he afraid while he was granted respite?'' He (peace be upon him) said: 'That some of his extremities would be cut off.'
ai.seo_question: What did Iblis fear from Jibreel during the Battle of Badr?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the metaphysical dimension of the Battle of Badr, where Iblis actively worked to distort the Muslims' perception of reality by minimizing their numbers and exaggerating the enemy's strength. Although Iblis is granted respite until the Day of Judgment, the Archangel Jibreel’s strike demonstrates that his 'temporary' status does not grant immunity from divine punishment or physical affliction in the spiritual realm, as he feared having his limbs severed. This narrative underscores the Shia understanding of the unseen forces influencing historical events and the tangible nature of angelic intervention.
